              ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY’S COMMENTS
      ON THE PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDED 16 TAC §§25.192, 25.193
                           AND NEW 16 TAC §25.252


         Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) files these comments in response to the

Public Utility Commission of Texas’s (the “Commission”) proposal for publication of amended 16

Tex. Admin. Code (“TAC”) §§25.192 and 25.192, as well as new 16 TAC §25.252; issued in this

rulemaking proceeding on July 10, 2026. Please refer to Attachment 1 for a redline version of the

rule language proposed in this docket with all of Oncor’s comments incorporated. Oncor also

explains in Attachment 2 hereto its proposed edits for implementation of these rules. Oncor

appreciates the opportunity to assist with Staff’s efforts to amend the Commission’s transmission

cost recovery rules for consistency with Senate Bill 6 and emerging Texas policy for cost

responsibility for large computational load customers.

                                       I.       SUMMARY

       All large computational load customers (existing, new, or expanded) should pay

transmission charges based on contracted capacity for at least a 10-year period, irrespective of

whether they have energized or met their load ramp because the discrete characteristics of these

grid users warrant this approach to mitigate the risk of passing costs caused by large computational

loads to other ratepayers. The best way to implement this is a take-or-pay obligation, which

produces the following benefits:

       •   Right-sized interconnection requests. Tying the payment obligation to requested

           capacity gives loads full knowledge from the outset that their obligation is fixed to the

           level they ask the system to study, reducing speculative requests.

       •   Lower costs for others. Revenue collected on contracted capacity above actual

           consumption reduces the total cost responsibility allocated to others.

       •   A sustained payment obligation. A 10-year minimum term produces the longest-

           duration transmission payment commitment in the ERCOT market, protecting other

           ratepayers from increased costs while also setting a reasonable minimum period for

           large computational loads to pay to reserve non-utilized capacity.

       •   Capacity reservation without cost shifting. A large computational load that continues

           to pay may hold its reserved capacity through ramp delays, causing no harm to the grid

           or other ratepayers.

       •   No uneconomic demand reduction. Fixing charges to reserved capacity removes the

           incentive to curtail during peak intervals to avoid transmission charges.

§§25.192 AND 193; AND NEW 16 TAC §25.252 Page 1 of 42
                                                                                                   2
        •      Consistency with cost causation. Transmission upgrades do not serve a single purpose

              and their beneficiaries change over decades of use. It is thus inappropriate to assign

              individual cost responsibility for network upgrades that benefit all grid users.

The example below in Oncor’s response to Question 5, drawn from a transmission project in south

Dallas, shows that a properly designed minimum billing demand can generate revenue exceeding

the associated revenue requirement—reducing transmission costs for every other rate class

consistent with emerging Texas policy to protect other rate classes from the cost of the large

computational load build-out.

 II.        ONCOR’S RESPONSES TO ENUMERATED QUESTIONS FOR COMMENT

   1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions

       be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or

       different non coincident (“NCP”) demands?

       No. Oncor recommends that the values associated with the large computational load

minimum billing demand provisions not be differentiated based on the customer’s contracted peak

demand or NCP demand. The proposed rule should apply at least a 10-year uniform minimum

billing demand to all large computational load customers at or above the 75 megawatt (“MW”)

threshold established by the Commission under Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) 1

§37.0561(c), and that uniform treatment should be maintained. Oncor’s response to Question 4

includes applicable legal support justifying separate rate treatment for large computational loads.

       A uniform minimum billing demand for large computational loads is consistent with cost

causation. Section 6(b) of Senate Bill 6 directs the Commission to ensure that its retail ratemaking

practices “appropriately charge[] the system costs that are caused by each customer class.” The


       1
           Public Utility Regulatory Act, Tex. Util. Code §§ 11.001-66.017.
ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDED 16 TAC
§§25.192 AND 193; AND NEW 16 TAC §25.252 Page 2 of 42
                                                                                                   3
 transmission system must be planned and built to serve large computational load customers at their

contracted peak demand, and each MW of contracted capacity imposes substantially the same

planning and construction obligation on utilities and the same cost on the system regardless of the

total size of the requesting load. Differentiating the minimum billing demand values by customer

size would introduce distinctions that are not grounded in differences in the costs these customers

cause the system. Because all large computational load customers above 75 MW (whether existing,

new, or expanded) impose substantially the same per-MW planning obligation, they share similar

cost profiles and should pay rates designed in the same manner—consistent with the principle of

horizontal equity articulated in the Commission Staff’s May 2026 Evaluation of Transmission Cost

Recovery (“Staff’s May Report”). 2 As Staff noted, discrimination among customers within that

class is “undue” when rate differences “are not supported by legitimate distinctions in cost

causation or other reasonable policy objectives.” A uniform minimum billing demand gives effect

to that principle.

        Introducing differentiated values for large load minimum billing demand based on load

size would also undermine the ratemaking principle of simplicity and understandability that

Commission Staff identified as a guiding principle for evaluating cost recovery methodologies,

and which if unchecked will increase litigation costs, which are ultimately borne by customers. 3 A

tiered minimum billing demand would require ongoing classification of customers into size bands,

create disputes with customers near the threshold between tiers, and introduce administrative

complexity in billing systems. Simplicity and understandability of billing classifications and




        2
          Evaluation of Transmission Cost Recovery, Project No. 58484, Staff Memo and Draft Report at 21-22
(May 4, 2026).
        3
          Staff’s May Report at 20.
ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDED 16 TAC
§§25.192 AND 193; AND NEW 16 TAC §25.252 Page 3 of 42
                                                                                                              4
 methodology underscore the need for the Commission to maintain a uniform minimum billing

demand for all large computational load customers.

   2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be: a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;

       b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or c. extended to a longer time period?

       Oncor recommends that the large load minimum billing demand be fixed for at least a 10-

year period and not reduced in phases or extended. Today, no loads are required to take power from

the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. (“ERCOT”) system for a specified period. Oncor is

cognizant of the political guidance from Senate Bill 6 and other sources that large loads who will

require higher costs for service need to have a long-term commitment to pay transmission rates,

and believes that a 10-year single term is sufficient.

       A ten-year term balances the need to impose a minimum billing requirement of substantial

duration to protect other ratepayers while also preventing large computational loads from holding

excessive non-utilized capacity for an unreasonable period. Further, a ten-year term captures the

initial full revenue requirement associated with the facilities, which drops as the asset is

depreciated due to less return, taxes, and other factors. Over time, ongoing load growth further

reduces the rate impact of the facilities and so capturing the initial ten years, at minimum,

appropriately protects other ratepayers. Oncor proposes extensive modification to new substantive

rule 25.252 to achieve this balance. If a contractual rate structure with at least a 10-year term is

adopted, it would be the longest payment obligation adopted for ERCOT transmission charges.

Today, loads are obligated to post security under interconnection agreements until they reach their

load ramps. At that point, security is released, and the load is responsible for payment of

transmission rates consistent with its energy usage on the Coincident Peaks (“CPs”). There is no

obligation to continue taking service beyond that point or to ever use the contracted capacity level

ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDED 16 TAC
§§25.192 AND 193; AND NEW 16 TAC §25.252 Page 4 of 42
                                                                                                   5
 that the system was built to meet. Among other significant customer and market protections,

Oncor’s proposed modifications to new rule 25.252 significantly expand that obligation and apply

it to both new and existing large computational load customers, thereby uniformly implementing

the take-or-pay concept. Oncor’s proposed modifications to these subsections are explained in

detail in Section V. below.

       The minimum billing demand should remain constant throughout the 10-year minimum

period and should not step down or phase out. The transmission facilities built to serve a large

computational load customer remain fully used and useful to that customer over time, and the

system planning obligation created by the customer’s contracted peak demand does not diminish

in phases. Further, phasing down the minimum billing demand over the applicable period would

progressively shift infrastructure costs caused by the large computational load customer to other

ratepayers without any corresponding reduction in the burden that customer’s contracted capacity

places on the system. A stepped or declining minimum billing demand would also require utilities

to maintain and manage rate changes at prescribed intervals for each large computational load

customer, creating bespoke billing logic for what will be a large and growing number of customers.

This would add complexity and costs. A phased reduction would also be contrary to the rate

stability principle. Under a phased reduction, other customer classes’ share of system costs would

increase each time a large computational load customer’s minimum billing demand steps down.

This creates instability or fluctuation in rates, impacting customers’ “ability to make rational

economic decisions when considering long-term investments in energy efficiency or demand

reduction technologies.” 4




       4
           Staff’s May Report at 21.
ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDED 16 TAC
§§25.192 AND 193; AND NEW 16 TAC §25.252 Page 5 of 42
                                                                                                 6
         Chairman Gleeson’s July 17, 2026 response (“Chairman’s July Letter”) to the Governor’s

June 10, 2026 directive (“Governor’s June Letter”) confirms that the Commission’s objective is to

require these large consumers to “begin paying transmission charges as soon as capacity becomes

available, even if they have not energized.” A phased reduction is inconsistent with that objective

because it would allow a large computational load customer to pay for progressively less capacity

over time despite continuing to reserve—and require the system to maintain and make available—

the full contracted capacity for that customer. By contrast, a fixed minimum billing demand for at

least 10 years ensures the large load customer pays for the capacity the system was built to deliver

and is long enough to ensure the customer remains in Texas. After at least 10 years, the customer

should transition to paying transmission rates on the same basis as other customers, which the

Commission envisions as billing based on a 12CP basis. Oncor also recommends that any reserved

capacity should at that time cease to be reserved and be made available to other customers.

        Oncor therefore recommends that the Commission reject a phased or declining minimum

billing demand and maintain a fixed minimum billing demand for at least a 10-year period.

    3. Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand

        lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large

        load minimum billing demand: (a) reflect a “ratcheted” demand; or (b) be based on

        a “weighted average” minimum billing demand?

        No. Simplicity and cost causation both suggest that the customer’s requested demand is the

best metric of rate setting.

        The transmission system is planned and built to serve a large computational load customer

at its full contracted peak demand. The Governor’s June Letter requires the Commission to

“prevent data centers from shifting development risks and costs onto Texans” and to “require data

ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDED 16 TAC
§§25.192 AND 193; AND NEW 16 TAC §25.252 Page 6 of 42
                                                                                                   7
 centers to pay for all of their electric infrastructure costs.” Neither a ratcheted demand or NCP

demand accomplish this goal because the system is built to serve a large computational load

customer’s contracted-for capacity. Either alternative approach would be inconsistent with the

Governor’s directive.

       Staff’s May Report recommended a minimum demand charge specifically because it

“would incent large load customers to request only capacity that the large load customer reasonably

expects to use and would discourage large load customers from requesting service for outsized

amounts of capacity.” Staff further concluded that a minimum demand charge “puts the financial

risk of a large load project not materializing on project developers instead of other ratepayers.” If

a large computational load customer can pay for only 50 or 75 percent of its contracted capacity,

the deterrent to speculative or oversized interconnection requests from large computational loads

is proportionally weakened, and the financial risk of a data center project failing to materialize is

shifted back to other ratepayers in proportion to the discount. This outcome is contrary to Staff’s

recommendation and the Governor’s directive.

       A weighted-average approach is also inconsistent with the ratemaking principles of

simplicity and understandability. A weighted-average minimum billing demand, particularly one

in which the percentage weighting declines in phases over time, would be overly burdensome and

administratively complex to configure in utility billing systems. Each large computational load

customer would be billed on a different blended rate in any given month depending on where it

falls in its phase-down schedule, creating bespoke billing logic for every customer in the class.

This introduces variability into the Transmission Cost Recovery Factor (“TCRF”) process, as

billing units for large loads could be determined by any one of three metrics in a given month,




ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDED 16 TAC
§§25.192 AND 193; AND NEW 16 TAC §25.252 Page 7 of 42
                                                                                                    8
 injecting unnecessary complexity and uncertainty into the design of rates for all customer classes.

This outcome also presents rate stability issues.

        Finally, requiring payment of transmission charges at the full contracted demand level—

rather than a discounted percentage—is consistent with the Chairman’s July Letter representing to

the Governor that the Commission is “[r]equiring large consumers of electricity to pay upfront the

direct costs to interconnect their facilities and begin paying transmission charges as soon as

capacity becomes available, even if they have not energized.”

    4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as

        an entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection

        Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power

        electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and

        cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include

        applicable legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large

        computational loads?

        Yes. Oncor recommends that separate rate treatment should be applied to existing, new,

behind-the-meter, and expanded large computational loads. The characteristics of large

computational loads—their unprecedented scale, the speed at which they seek to interconnect, how

they functionally behave on the transmission system, and the disproportionate transmission

infrastructure investment they require—distinguish them from other large load customers in ways

that are directly relevant to cost causation and that justify a distinct rate treatment.

        PURA does not prohibit discrimination among customers; it prohibits unreasonable

discrimination. Specifically, PURA §36.003 requires that rates be just and reasonable, and “not

unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory but sufficient, equitable, and consistent in

ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDED 16 TAC
§§25.192 AND 193; AND NEW 16 TAC §25.252 Page 8 of 42
                                                                                                     9
 application to each class of consumer.” The operative qualifier is “unreasonably.” The statute

expressly contemplates that rates will differ among classes of consumers and requires only that

rates be consistent in application within each class. The Legislature reinforced this framework in

Senate Bill 6, Section 6(b), which directs the Commission to evaluate whether its retail ratemaking

practices ensure that “transmission cost recovery appropriately charges the system costs that are

caused by each customer class.” The reference to costs caused by “each customer class”

presupposes that the Commission may define classes according to the costs their members cause.

Further, PURA §36.001 grants the Commission authority to establish and regulate rates and to

“adopt rules for determining the classification of customers and services and the applicability of

rates.” Separate rate treatment dictated by cost causation for large computational loads is therefore

a reasonable distinction, expressly authorized by statute. Thus, Oncor submits that all existing,

new, and expanded large computational loads should be subject to these rules, with an appropriate

carve out for existing large computational loads explained in Section V below.

       The Texas Supreme Court has confirmed that discrimination between customers is

permissible, as long as the discrimination is not unreasonable, and this logic should extend to the

issue of large computational loads now at issue. For example, in Tex. Alarm & Signal Ass’n v.

Pub. Util. Comm’n of Tex., when considering the Commission’s approval of a classification of a

particular type of service and the rate design applied to that classification, the Texas Supreme Court

explained that rate classifications and discrimination, which do not have to be based exclusively

on cost, can be based on several factors such as the cost of service, the purpose for which the

service or product is received, the quantity or amount received, the different character of the service

furnished, the time of its use, or any other matter which presents a substantial difference as a




ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDED 16 TAC
§§25.192 AND 193; AND NEW 16 TAC §25.252 Page 9 of 42
                                                                                                     10
 ground of distinction. 5 Additionally, in Pub. Util. Comm’n of Tex. v. AT&T Communications of

the Sw., the Texas Supreme Court found the Commission had acted within its authority by

designating interexchange carriers (i.e., long-distance telephone companies independent of the

Bell operating companies) as a distinct class of customers separate from the other classes of

customers of the local exchange companies, noting that the Commission found that the manner in

which interexchange carriers were using the networks at issue was fundamentally different than

the use made by other customers, along with other differences. 6

        Staff’s own analytical framework in Staff’s May Report is consistent with this precedent.

It outlines the principle of vertical equity, which “requires that customers with different profiles

who impose different costs on the system should face different rates.” Staff further explained that

rate differences among customers “are not inherently problematic,” and that discrimination

becomes undue only “when rate differences are not supported by legitimate distinctions in cost

causation or other reasonable policy objectives.” Staff also cautioned against “cost recovery

methodologies that fail to recognize meaningful differences in cost responsibility among

customers with distinct load characteristics and the effects that these differences have on the

system.” In light of these principles, the failure to distinguish large computational loads from other

large loads would be inappropriate because it would assign identical rate treatment to customers

with materially different cost and load profiles.

        Large computational loads are quick to market relative to traditional industrial

development and have sensitive electronics which place unique demand on the system. Their

power electronic characteristics also present complex grid operation considerations that may

Caldwell v. City of Abilene, 260 S.W.2d 712, 714 (Tex. Civ. App.—Eastland 1953, writ ref’d)).
        6
          See Pub. Util. Comm’n of Tex. v. AT&T Communications of the Sw., 777 S.W.2d 363, 366 (Tex. 1989).
ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDED 16 TAC
§§25.192 AND 193; AND NEW 16 TAC §25.252 Page 10 of 42
                                                                                                          11
 require either the load or the transmission system to add equipment to manage reliability risks.

These are precisely the “meaningful differences in cost responsibility among customers with

distinct load characteristics” that Staff’s May Report identified as requiring recognition in rate

design, including imposing a take-or-pay mechanism and minimum billing demand. These

proposed rules should reflect this approach.

       The Governor and the Chairman have both identified large computational loads

specifically, not large loads generally, as the source of the cost pressure this rulemaking addresses.

The Governor’s June Letter instructs the Commission to ensure that “data centers’

interconnections will result in reduced residential electrical bills,” to “require data centers to pay

for all of their electric infrastructure costs to ensure that no residential ratepayer is burdened by

those costs,” and to consider “measures to prevent data centers from shifting development risks

and costs onto Texans” (emphasis added). The Chairman’s July Letter confirmed that the

Commission is acting to ensure that “the costs associated with serving new data center

development are appropriately aligned with investment and do not burden residential and small

business ratepayers” (emphasis added). A rule that applies undifferentiated treatment to all large

loads ignores those directives and risks imposing collateral consequences on industrial and

commercial customers that have operated within traditional interconnection processes for decades

without generating comparable cost pressure.

       Approved filings for utilities operating outside the ERCOT region but subject to the

Commission’s retail ratemaking authority also demonstrate that separate treatment for large

computational loads specifically, and any distinguishable rate class generally, is consistent with

applicable Commission law and precedent. For example, El Paso Electric Company has applied

§§25.192 AND 193; AND NEW 16 TAC §25.252 Page 11 of 42
                                                                                                    12
 for approval of Schedule No. 27, High Load Factor Large Power Service Rate. 7 El Paso Electric

states that it expects a very large customer eligible for service under the new tariff to “have their

own rate class for cost allocation and ratemaking purposes,” and that the determination whether a

combined rate class or customer-specific classes is appropriate would be made “consistent with

standard practice.” El Paso Electric’s tariff amendment application follows the Commission’s

approval of customer-specific rate schedules for a single data center customer in Docket No.

56903. 8 The Commission concluded as a matter of law in that docket that a discrete rate schedule

for that 100 MW large computational load was in accordance with PURA §36.003(b), and that the

rates approved in that order are not unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory and

are sufficient, equitable, and consistent in application to each class of consumer. 9 More generally,

Entergy Texas Inc.’s riders to its rate schedules discriminate between seasonal customers and

higher education institutions versus the remainder of the applicable rate class as a whole. 10

Reasonable distinctions among customers within rate classes and discrete rate classes for specific

classes of customers are nothing new to the Commission, and thus the Commission should exercise

its discretion to do so with respect to large computational loads.

    5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include

       transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to

       serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

       No. The definition of transmission interconnection costs should not be broadened to

include transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to serve the

transmission capacity needs of a particular load. The definition should be limited to the direct

transmission interconnection costs that only the interconnecting large computational load will

utilize, and the Commission should further clarify that system upgrades are not direct transmission

interconnection costs.

       Broadening the definition would be inconsistent with the structure of the Commission’s

pending interconnection standards rule. In Project No. 58481, proposed §25.194 treats direct

interconnection costs and system upgrades as separate and distinct categories subject to different

financial mechanisms. Under proposed §25.194(f)(9)(A), direct interconnection costs “include all

costs associated with facilities built to interconnect the large load customer to the existing ERCOT

system, including radial lines and substation upgrades necessary to interconnect the new large load

customer,” and are recovered through Contributions In Aid of Construction (“CIAC”) paid as a

direct cash payment. System upgrades, by contrast, are addressed separately under proposed

§25.194(f)(10), which requires the large load customer to post financial security—not CIAC—for

“system upgrades that are necessary to reliably serve the large load customer.” That separation

reflects a determination that facilities dedicated exclusively to a single interconnecting customer

are treated differently from upgrades to the shared network. Expanding the definition of

transmission interconnection costs in these rules to encompass batch study upgrades would inaptly

collapse a distinction that §25.194 creates. Such a change would also be inconsistent with the fact

ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDED 16 TAC
§§25.192 AND 193; AND NEW 16 TAC §25.252 Page 13 of 42
                                                                                                  14
 that ERCOT’s transmission network is not dedicated to any single customer; it is a common use

open-sourced network that is paid by and benefits all electric customers.

       Staff’s May Report reached the same conclusion, observing that although expanding

interconnection costs to include system upgrades “is an appealing approach that seems consistent

with cost causation and equitable ratemaking principles,” in practice “such an approach comes

with many challenges and would be complex to administer.” Staff identified the assignment of

costs based on cost causation principles as a central challenge, explaining that “[p]ower flows on

the transmission system do not serve just one entity or even a handful of entities” and that “the

direction of power flows is not consistent, making it difficult to identify the beneficiary of

individual transmission facilities in a limiting manner.” Staff further questioned “whether a system

upgrade that is identified in the batch study process can be attributed to a large load customer when

the system upgrade will serve other loads on the system in order to free a path for existing power

flows to the large load customer seeking interconnection.” Staff’s analysis is directly responsive

to the question posed here, and it counsels against broadening the definition.

       The batch study process itself confirms the point. The batch study is not limited to large

loads. All loads are evaluated in the batch process, and the transmission projects that emerge from

a batch study are expected to serve the aggregate needs of the system as studied, not the needs of

any single customer in isolation. When multiple loads are modeled together in a single batch,

attributing a resulting network upgrade to one participant rather than another is problematic, and

any attempt to do so will produce contested determinations that delay the construction of the very

upgrades the batch process identified as necessary (which the batch process was designed to

expedite). Indeed, the Commission approved ERCOT Planning Guide Revision Request 145 in

June 2026 to establish the Batch Zero process so that ERCOT could “determine how much load

ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDED 16 TAC
§§25.192 AND 193; AND NEW 16 TAC §25.252 Page 14 of 42
                                                                                                   15
 can be reliably served by location and year, allocate available transmission capacity to these

projects, and identify transmission upgrades needed for committed projects.” Converting that

system-wide planning output into a customer-specific cost assignment mechanism would

introduce modeling and allocation disputes into a process designed to accelerate, not encumber,

the interconnection of new load.

       Broadening the definition would also conflict with the postage stamp methodology that

PURA prescribes and that this rulemaking does not disturb. PURA §35.004(d) establishes postage

stamp pricing for wholesale transmission service, and Staff’s May Report placed that methodology

outside the scope of this rulemaking, noting it “is not addressed in Senate Bill 6; therefore, this

report assumes there will be no changes to this principle.” Directly assigning batch study upgrade

costs to individual loads would thus inaptly depart from postage stamp ratemaking.              The

methodology should also remain undisturbed because transmission upgrades are long-lived assets

whose beneficiaries change over their service lives; upgrades originally built for one purpose

decades ago today may serve other grid purposes later. Thus, assigning the full cost of a network

upgrade to the load whose interconnection request happened to trigger its identification would

inappropriately attribute to that customer the cost of an asset that benefits all system users for

decades.

       Finally, broadening the definition would expand the portion of utility facilities recovered

through CIAC, which operates as a direct offset to rate base and denies the utility any return on

facilities it constructs, manages, and maintains. Utilities would thus be at risk of under-recovery

under a broadened definition. As Staff’s May Report identified, a rate is not reasonable if it “fails

to approximately recover approved costs or fails to provide the utility with a reasonable

opportunity to earn a reasonable return on its invested capital.” Substantially increasing the volume

ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDED 16 TAC
§§25.192 AND 193; AND NEW 16 TAC §25.252 Page 15 of 42
                                                                                                   16
 of transmission network investment excluded from rate base would undermine that principle at a

time when utilities are being asked to raise unprecedented levels of capital to fund a grid buildout

that will benefit economic development in Texas, which in turn benefits all.

        The difference between recovering network investment through CIAC and recovering it

through rates tied to contracted capacity is not academic, as a recent Oncor project illustrates. In

2024, Oncor submitted a project to the ERCOT Regional Planning Group to increase capacity in

the south Dallas area by 4 GW. The cost of the project as proposed was $1.2 billion. The

                                       I.       SUMMARY

       All large computational load customers (existing, new, or expanded) should pay

transmission charges based on contracted capacity for at least a 10-year period, irrespective of

whether they have energized or met their load ramp because the discrete characteristics of these

grid users warrant this approach to mitigate the risk of passing costs caused by large computational

loads to other ratepayers. The best way to implement this is a take-or-pay obligation, which

produces the following benefits:

       •   Right-sized interconnection requests. Tying the payment obligation to requested

           capacity gives loads full knowledge from the outset that their obligation is fixed to the

           level they ask the system to study, reducing speculative requests.

       •   Lower costs for others. Revenue collected on contracted capacity above actual

           consumption reduces the total cost responsibility allocated to others.

       •   A sustained payment obligation. A 10-year minimum term produces the longest-

           duration transmission payment commitment in the ERCOT market, protecting other

           ratepayers from increased costs while also setting a reasonable minimum period for

           large computational loads to pay to reserve non-utilized capacity.

       •   Capacity reservation without cost shifting. A large computational load that continues

           to pay may hold its reserved capacity through ramp delays, causing no harm to the grid

           or other ratepayers.

       •   No uneconomic demand reduction. Fixing charges to reserved capacity removes the

           incentive to curtail during peak intervals to avoid transmission charges.
